population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 79M of ~267M US adults are currently on an incretin (29.7%), for any indication. Age check: 0.20×17.5 + 0.33×32 + 0.24×42 + 0.23×24 = 3.5 + 10.56 + 10.08 + 5.52 ≈ 29.7. Income thirds (34/31/24) average to 29.7. Cheap generics narrowed the gap, from an 11-point to a 10-point spread with a much higher floor; the bottom third now uses mostly $49–69 generic semaglutide and cycles more. Cycling arithmetic: ever 37.5% − current 29.7% = 7.8 pp of adults who used and are off now (~21M people). The two-year influx of ~13.5 pp new users dilutes the restarter share among current users to ~28% (0.28×29.7 ≈ 8.3 pp), and ~25% of those currently off had cycled before (0.25×7.8 ≈ 1.95 pp), so (8.3 + 1.95)/37.5 ≈ 27% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once. Payer mix of the 79M: diabetes-, cardiac-, renal-, MASH-, OSA- or AUD-coded coverage across all payers ~24M (AUD-coded ~1.5M of these, mostly since the May 2030 label); employer obesity coverage ~9M; Medicare obesity-only Continuity Model ~1.6M; Medicaid obesity ~1.8M; brand cash (retatrutide, Zepbound, oral amycretin, Foundayo, Wegovy pill via TrumpRx/direct) ~8M; US generic semaglutide paid in cash ~30.8M; gray market ~3.8M. These sum to 79M. Of the cash-generic users, ~1.2M are on low-dose 'craving/calm' telehealth subscriptions, not weight plans. About 21M adults have used and stopped; ~6M of them stopped because of a coverage change or lockout, and more now stop because they 'got where they wanted' at $49 and plan to restart. Pediatric: ~1.2% of under-18s (~0.9M), mostly aged 12–17 on generic semaglutide paid by parents in cash. Under-12 use is still specialist-only. Roughly 40% of US children live in a household where at least one adult is on the drug. Never-users with obesity (~25M adults) are now mainly people who decline the drug, people who can't sustain $50/month, and people who can't tolerate it, not people priced out by $199.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the CMS GLP-1 Continuity Model runs unchanged at ~$245/month paid and a ~$50 beneficiary copay, with the ≥80% refill-adherence condition, the ≥5% loss at 6 months and the 12-month lockout on lapse. The model's rate is defined on brand products. Enrollment is flat at ~1.6M obesity-only beneficiaries, because some eligible seniors now buy generic semaglutide at $49 cash, roughly the copay, to avoid the lockout rules. Spending: 1.6M × $245 × 12 ≈ $4.7B/yr. Medicaid: the same 19 states cover obesity for ~1.8M enrollees. Ordinary mandatory generic substitution moved ~60% of semaglutide fills to generic at ~$60 including dispensing by late 2030. Run rate: 1.8M × (0.4×$245 + 0.6×$60) × 12 = 1.8M × $134 × 12 ≈ $2.9B/yr gross, federal share at ~65% FMAP ≈ $1.9B. The seven adherence waivers continue.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and most of Southeast Asia have generic semaglutide (India ~$8–40/month); generic oral semaglutide is sold in India since 2028 and launched in Brazil in 2029. Indian manufacturers holding US settlement licences now export finished product legally into the US.
access.note: Price follows generic_collapse. A Sep 2029 patent settlement let licensed generic semaglutide injection enter the US in Jan 2030, about 22 months before patent expiry. Novo launched an authorised generic the same day. By mid-2030 cash generic semaglutide (all doses including 2.4 mg) sells at $49–69/month at retail, with low-dose discount pharmacy pricing from $39. Brand prices responded: Zepbound vials $199–249, Foundayo $99, Wegovy pill $129, oral amycretin $199 direct. Retatrutide fell to $349, the premium exception. There is no generic tirzepatide, oral semaglutide or retatrutide in the US. Employer weight coverage is 43% (Business Group on Health, 2030), essentially unchanged; most plans that cover it moved to generic-first step therapy. Gray market: personal-importation telehealth lost its price advantage, and most platforms switched to dispensing US generic. The remaining ~3.8M gray users are mostly on research-peptide retatrutide and cagrilintide ($120–200/month) or uninsured users of Mexican and Indian product near the borders. New starts are ~55% oral, driven by oral amycretin and Foundayo.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, plus US generics and Novo authorised generic since Jan 2030)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro; brand only)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, Lilly)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular co-agonist, daily oral (oral amycretin, Novo; approved Apr 2030)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: smoking and nicotine-vaping cessation in adults with overweight or obesity (semaglutide, Sep 2028)
alcohol use disorder in adults, regardless of BMI (semaglutide 2.4 mg, May 2030; ASAM and APA guidelines list it as a first-line option alongside naltrexone)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: generic semaglutide for AUD: generics carve the new indication out of their labels (Novo holds 3-year exclusivity on it), but most AUD prescriptions are written for generic anyway
low-dose 'craving, calm and focus' subscriptions through telehealth wellness brands, sold as programmes rather than as an indication
nicotine cessation in normal-weight smokers and vapers
gambling and compulsive shopping reduction, discussed in clinics but with no RCTs
research-peptide retatrutide and cagrilintide stacks in gym and 'recomposition' communities
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Oral parity is realised by oral amycretin, honouring the 'next_gen_launch' driver: phase 3, filed Mar 2029, approved Apr 2030 (13 months after filing). It gives ~22% mean loss at 68 weeks, matching tirzepatide but not retatrutide's ~29%, and its GI tolerability is similar to injectables. It removes the needle as a reason not to start. Survodutide was filed Feb 2029; its FDA decision is due early 2031, so it is not on the market. MariTide (monthly injectable) finished phase 3 and was filed Jun 2030; it is not on the market. Semaglutide AUD: phase 3 read out Mar 2029, with about 1.4 fewer heavy-drinking days per week vs placebo, comparable to naltrexone and additive in a subgroup. The sNDA was filed Jul 2029 and approved May 2030. The global incretin market is ~$120B (2030): US unit volume is up ~65% on 2028 while US revenue is roughly flat, because per-unit price fell by more than half. Novo is pivoting its brand business to oral amycretin; Lilly's revenue rests on tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Oral amycretin's GI profile is similar to injectables. Cheap generic self-titration, often skipping steps, adds early dropouts.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic label 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis'; generics carry identical labels.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid loss; retatrutide real-world incidence is in line with the early signal.
Still no causal confirmation; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL ongoing, first bellwether trial postponed to 2031.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Persistent concern at retatrutide-scale loss and in older adults. Bone-density association in women over 60 is still at cohort-abstract stage, with no new signal. Lean-mass preservation has become a private, paid service.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Retatrutide label recommends resistance exercise and protein counselling; no class warning.
EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; no US class label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new evidence, including in the AUD trial population, which had higher baseline psychiatric morbidity.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still unquantified as a harm, and now sold as a benefit. Telehealth brands cite user surveys in which roughly 60% report 'less wanting' or 'a quieter mind'. No trial uses a validated anhedonia scale as an endpoint; the AUD programme measured craving, not hedonic capacity.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. The FTC opened inquiries into two wellness subscription advertisers over unsubstantiated 'focus' claims; no action taken.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About half of lost weight is regained within a year. At $49, more stops are voluntary 'pauses' with a planned restart, while coverage and Continuity Model lockouts still drive involuntary stops.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; it still underpins the Medicare and Medicaid adherence conditions.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reports continue at retatrutide-level intake reduction and among low-income generic users eating one meal a day.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; professional societies recommend baseline and annual labs, which cash-generic users mostly skip.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescents; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The first adolescent cohorts (2023–25 starters) begin crossing five years. ~27% of ever-users have cycled. The Sentinel cycling study is enrolling, with no results.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; FDA Sentinel cycling study ongoing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The total of adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~6,500, but the yearly rate fell in 2030 as cheap legal generic displaced imports. Research-peptide retatrutide is now the majority of new reports.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion stands; import alerts stand; personal-importation enforcement mostly unpursued.

safety_ledger.effect: Acquired olfactory and taste dysfunction (hyposmia/dysgeusia) after ≥5 years of continuous GLP-1 RA use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal. A US claims replication was underpowered and inconclusive. Confounding by diabetes duration still unresolved; HR ~1.5 and ~2–3 per 1,000 person-years excess remain the reference figures.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA PRAC (2029) asked marketing authorisation holders for a post-authorisation safety study rather than a label change; FDA Sentinel review continues; no label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Mostly mild and dose-related; also frequent in research-peptide users who skip titration.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~40% of US households. Snack and confectionery unit volumes are down a further ~3–4% since 2028 (~7% below 2026), and sugary drinks ~6% below 2026. Growth sits in protein, fibre, small formats and 'one-meal' nutrient-dense products aimed at cash-generic users who eat little. Private-label snack plants continue closing in Ohio, Indiana and Iowa. Big CPG firms treat incretin adoption as a permanent demand baseline and cut guidance once, not repeatedly.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down another ~6% over two years and beer ~3%. The May 2030 AUD label and generic price put the drug in front of the heaviest-drinking decile, who account for most volume. Neighbourhood bars and late-night on-premise venues are closing in older industrial cities. Non-alc grows. Two sportsbook operators and a casino REIT add 'incretin adoption' to risk factors after anecdotal handle declines among older bettors.

restaurants.state: Traffic is down ~1–2%. Half-portion menus are standard. Bar-and-grill chains lose alcohol attach rates and push protein bowls. High-end tasting menus are fine, because small and expensive suits the top-tier eater.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting. Mid-market retailers face re-sizing churn as cycling users move between sizes. Fitted performance wear and 'structured' menswear tailored to show shoulders and arms grow at the premium end, because muscle, not slimness, is the visible status cue.

fitness.state: Strength-training studios, private coaching and DEXA body-composition scanning grow fast in high-income metros. Big-box low-cost gyms are flat; their members are on generic sema and mostly don't lift. 'Muscle-preservation' packages bundle retatrutide or oral amycretin prescriptions with coaching at $300–600/month.

insurance.state: No structural change in who pays. Employer weight coverage is 43%; plans that cover it moved to generic-first step therapy. Benefit consultants pitch generic-only obesity coverage at roughly $60/member/month on users, but plan designs are set a year ahead and few employers re-added coverage before the 2031 plan year. Pharmacy trend fell to ~4% as generic substitution cut diabetes-coded semaglutide spend. ~1 in 5 large self-funded employers still run BMI surcharges, and some now accept a cash generic pharmacy receipt as 'adherence'.

pharma.state: Volume is growing and price is collapsing. Lilly dominates branded revenue. Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell sharply after the settlement, and its authorised generic captures a share of generic volume. Licensed generic makers, including two Indian firms, run thin margins at high volume. The industry is adapting, not growing in US dollars.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness is cheap, so it no longer signals much. Visible muscle, posture, good skin after loss and the absence of 'reta face' sag (fixed by $8–15k skin-tightening procedures) signal money and time. A lean body without muscle reads as '$49 thin'. A larger body now reads as refusal, intolerance, or a lapse between cycles.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Body shape reads as income in a new way. The top tier is retatrutide or oral amycretin plus a coach, protein, DEXA scans and cosmetic finishing. The middle is brand pills or generic sema with a big-box gym membership. The bottom third is generic sema bought in cash and paused when money runs short, with the weight cycling to match. In Columbus, Ohio, warehouse and distribution workers are about as likely as Upper Arlington professionals to be on the drug, but their bodies look different in ways co-workers can name.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are smaller everywhere. 'One good meal' culture spreads among low-income generic users. Church potlucks in Black congregations in Atlanta and Mennonite communities in Lancaster County stay deliberate sites of abundance and pride. 'Made Whole' congregations in Texas and Oklahoma split over whether fasting on a drug counts as fasting.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles in New York, LA and Austin list 'lifts' and training splits more than 'on it/off it'. Being on the drug is assumed. Mismatched desire in couples is now discussed through the marketing vocabulary ('I'm just quieter now').
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: The AUD label completes the official story: wanting too much is a treatable condition, and wanting less is health. Fat-liberation groups in Oakland and Atlanta shift their argument from access to class ('they made thin cheap so they could sell muscle'). MAHA influencers attack teen use and the 'calm' subscriptions. The groups still don't agree with each other.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Still not measured as a harm by any trial, registry or label. Telehealth brands now measure it as a benefit through their own surveys (~60% of users report 'less wanting'). About 1.2M adults hold low-dose 'craving and calm' subscriptions, which are sold as programmes rather than weight treatment. The concept is visible and the costs are still not.
interior_life.framing: Feature. 'Quiet mind', 'freedom from craving' and 'calm focus' are advertising categories. The AUD and nicotine indications lend them medical credibility that the marketing borrows without stating.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Wellness vendors pitch 'craving-free focus' to employers, and a few tech and finance firms list subscription reimbursement in lifestyle-spending accounts, though none mandate it. Sales and hospitality managers say privately that 'everybody's even now'. Bartending and late-shift service jobs thin as on-premise drinking contracts.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Late-night culture keeps contracting in mid-size cities, as bars, bowling leagues and casino buses lose their older regulars. Comedians build sets around the 'quiet' subscriptions. Live music splits between high-sensation spectacle and seated, sober daytime shows. A small, celebrated genre of artists talks openly about coming off the drug 'to want things again'.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples therapists report clients using brand language to describe lower desire as contentment. Some couples schedule drug holidays around anniversaries and trips. Clinical literature still has no measured libido or attachment endpoint.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measured change in turnout in the 2030 midterms. Columnists on left and right argue about a 'quiet electorate' without data. MAHA candidates campaign against marketing 'calm' to teenagers, and the fight is about marketing, not the molecule.

state.regulatory_posture: Unchanged. The FDA is fast on approvals (oral amycretin, the AUD label) and passive on personal importation, research peptides and wellness-programme marketing. The FTC sends inquiry letters about 'focus' claims but takes no enforcement action. No new legislation or rulemaking on incretins this step.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Continuity Model continues at $245/$50 for ~1.6M, and Medicaid covers obesity in 19 states. TrumpRx lists brand cash prices; the administration claims credit for generic prices it did not set.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged rules, with more people in them. The Medicare and seven Medicaid waivers keep the ≥80% refill and ≥5% response conditions and the 12-month lockout. ~1 in 5 large self-funded employers keep BMI surcharges ($50–100/month), waived by biometric proof or verified adherence. Connected-pen apps and pharmacy cash-receipt uploads to wellness vendors are the verification route for the growing cash-generic population. Cheap cash generic also lets people leave public surveillance: some Medicare-eligible seniors buy outside the model to avoid the lockout.
state.workforce_or_military: Army and Air Force accession waivers for GLP-1-assisted body composition still require ≥6 months off-drug stability. TRICARE covers obesity use for active duty only under strict criteria. Recruiters report more applicants mid-pause.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US–India price gap collapsed from ~$199 vs ~$15 to ~$49 vs ~$15. Indian firms holding settlement licences ship legally to US pharmacies, while import alerts on unlicensed API shippers remain. Tariff-relief bargaining shifts to tirzepatide and oral products.

events.event: Novo's phase 3 trial of semaglutide 2.4 mg in alcohol use disorder meets its primary endpoint, cutting heavy-drinking days by about 1.4 per week versus placebo; an sNDA follows in July.

Novo Nordisk settles US patent litigation with a group of generic filers including Viatris and two Indian manufacturers, licensing generic semaglutide injection from January 2030, about 22 months before patent expiry, and announces an authorised generic of its own.

Generic semaglutide launches at US pharmacies; by June cash prices for all doses sit at $49–69 a month, Lilly cuts Foundayo to $99 and Zepbound vials to $199, and telehealth importers switch to dispensing US generic.

FDA approves Novo's oral amycretin, a daily pill producing about 22% average weight loss at 68 weeks, matching injectable tirzepatide; it launches at $199 a month direct, and oral share of new starts passes half.
FDA approves semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in adults regardless of weight; generic makers carve the indication out of their labels, and ASAM lists the drug as a first-line option within weeks.

Telehealth brand Stillwater Health reports 1.2 million subscribers to 'Quiet', a $59-a-month low-dose generic semaglutide programme advertised for 'calm, focus and freedom from craving'; the FTC sends inquiry letters to it and one rival, and DEXA-scan chains report body-composition scans up threefold in a year in New York, the Bay Area and Austin.

open_tensions: Medicare pays $245 a month under the Continuity Model for drugs that sell for $49 in cash, and the beneficiary copay is now about the generic cash price. Seniors are starting to leave the surveillance-and-lockout system to pay cash, and nobody has decided whether the model should follow them.

Employers have a $60 option and haven't taken it. Coverage held at 43% through 2030, and the 2031 plan year will show whether cheap generics bring obesity coverage back or confirm that weight treatment is a private cash purchase.

Reward blunting is now a product with 1.2M subscribers and a borrowed medical vocabulary from the AUD and nicotine labels, and still nobody measures its costs. The first adolescent users cross five years of exposure just as cheap generics push teenage use up.

Thinness is no longer scarce, so class has moved to muscle, skin and continuity. The bottom third cycles on and off cash generic and its health effects are unstudied, while the top third buys retatrutide, coaching and cosmetic finishing.
still_true: The CMS Medicare GLP-1 Continuity Model still pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay, keeping the ≥80% refill-adherence condition, the ≥5% loss at 6 months and the 12-month lockout on lapse.
No FDA-approved generic tirzepatide exists in the US; Zepbound and Mounjaro remain brand-only.
The FDA's Jan 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels stands and has not been reinstated.
Texas's 2027 ban on BMI-based premium surcharges still covers only state-regulated plans, and about 1 in 5 large ERISA self-funded employers still run BMI surcharges of $50–100/month.
The Army and Air Force accession waivers still require recruits who reached standards on a GLP-1 to show ≥6 months of off-drug weight stability.

prose.headline: Forty-Nine-Dollar Thin: The Drug Got Cheap. Now You Can Read Someone's Income Off Their Shoulders.
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 nearly three American adults in ten are on an incretin drug, about 79 million people. Another 21 million have been on one and are off for now. Most of them plan to go back. Price is no longer what decides that. In September 2029 Novo Nordisk, losing ground to Lilly and its remaining exclusivity worth less every quarter, settled with a group of generic makers and let them sell semaglutide almost two years early. Generic semaglutide reached pharmacy shelves in January. By summer a month's supply cost $49 to $69 in cash, less than a phone bill, and the import-by-telehealth trade that had served six million people mostly turned into ordinary dispensing.

Almost nothing else about who pays has changed. Employers that dropped weight coverage have not brought it back, although a generic-only benefit would cost them little; plan designs are set a year ahead, and the 2031 renewals are the real test. Diabetics, heart patients and now problem drinkers are covered under their codes. Medicare still pays $245 a month through its adherence-policed Continuity Model, which means a senior's $50 copay is roughly what the same drug costs at the counter with no refill monitoring and no lockout. Some seniors have worked this out. Medicaid's cost fell without any policy change, through ordinary generic substitution at the pharmacy.

The needle is gone as an objection too. Novo's oral amycretin, approved in April, takes off about as much weight as injectable tirzepatide, and more than half of new patients now start on a pill. Lilly's retatrutide, at $349, is still the most effective drug available, and it has become the drug of the affluent.

That is where class has moved. When thinness was expensive it was a status marker. Now that anyone can be thin for $49, the body shows money in other ways: muscle kept through the loss, skin tightened afterwards, a coach, a DEXA scan every quarter, a lean body that holds its shape because the person never has to pause. In Columbus, distribution-centre workers are on the drug at nearly the rate of the lawyers in Upper Arlington, and anyone at a cookout can tell which is which. Strength studios and body-composition scan chains are booming in New York, the Bay Area and Austin. Big-box gyms are flat.

In May the FDA approved semaglutide for alcohol use disorder, for people of any weight. The addiction societies put it on the first line within weeks. Generic makers carved the new indication off their labels, and doctors prescribe the generic anyway. Spirits volumes fell another six percent. Neighbourhood bars in Toledo and Scranton are closing, and two sportsbooks have added the drug to their risk disclosures.

The effect that worried people in 2026, the flatness and the quieting of wanting, is now a product. A telehealth company called Stillwater sells 'Quiet', low-dose generic semaglutide for calm, focus and freedom from craving, to 1.2 million subscribers at $59 a month. Its advertisements never mention weight. The FTC has written letters to the company and taken no action. No trial measures what the effect costs, because every trial is built to measure what it cures.

No new safety signal appeared. The European review of lost smell after long use ended with a request for more study. The first teenagers who started in 2025 are reaching five years on the drug just as the cheap generic pushes teenage use past one percent. Snack volumes are down again, and so are plus-size store counts. Bowling leagues are thinning. The country is calmer and leaner, and it can see its class divisions more plainly than before.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Kowalczyk, 44, works as a shift lead at a distribution centre outside Columbus, Ohio. Her alarm goes at 4:40. The pen is in the butter compartment of the fridge. Generic semaglutide, two milligrams this month, she isn't sure of the brand. She paid $54 at Kroger on the 3rd and photographed the receipt for the wellness app, which waives the $85 monthly BMI surcharge as long as she keeps uploading.

At seven, Marisol, the floor supervisor, walks the line in a fitted quarter-zip, forearms like rope. She's on the expensive one and has a coach, everybody says. Dana's own arms are thin and soft. Her sister calls it forty-nine-dollar thin, and she means it kindly.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and gives the rest to Terrell, who stopped in March when his hours were cut. He's restarting Friday. 'Payday,' he says, like a man booking a dentist.

At home Rick is already on the porch with a seltzer. His union plan covered his prescription in June, once it was coded for drinking. He hasn't been to Mulligan's since. Mulligan's closed in September.

Their daughter Kayla, fifteen, asks again whether she can start. Half her volleyball team is on it. Dana says ask the doctor. Kayla says the doctor costs more than the pen.

They watch television without snacks. Rick laughs once. Around ten he says, not unhappily, 'You ever notice we don't really want anything anymore?'

Dana thinks about it, and then about the receipt she has to upload on the 3rd.
